blocks.text: A 44-year-old man, day one after a thoracotomy, rates his pain 2 out of 10 lying still but 9 out of 10 when asked to cough. He will not cough, his chest is filling with secretions, and his oxygen saturation is drifting down. How pain is relieved, delivered and measured decides whether he can breathe deeply enough to recover.

blocks.markdown: **Epidural analgesia (objective 1).** An epidural catheter placed in the epidural space delivers a continuous infusion (or intermittent boluses) of dilute local anaesthetic, often with a low-dose opioid, to block spinal nerve roots at the segmental level of the surgery. Thoracic epidurals suit thoracic and upper abdominal surgery and lumbar epidurals suit lower abdominal, pelvic and lower limb surgery, and labour. Epidural analgesia gives excellent dynamic analgesia (pain on movement and cough), which can help physiotherapy and may reduce pulmonary complications after major surgery. The block is assessed by sensory level (for example with cold) and by motor block (for example with the Bromage scale).

**Peripheral nerve blocks.** A single injection of local anaesthetic around a nerve or plexus (often under ultrasound guidance) gives analgesia for several hours, and a perineural catheter can extend this. Examples include interscalene block for shoulder surgery, femoral or adductor canal blocks for knee surgery, and fascia iliaca block for hip fracture. They spare opioids and avoid systemic effects but depend on the block reaching the correct territory.

rows: Major thoracic or abdominal surgery; labour
Dynamic analgesia, titratable, can run for days
Hypotension, motor block, urinary retention, pruritus (with opioid), patchy or failed block, dural puncture headache, total spinal, epidural haematoma or abscess, local anaesthetic toxicity
Limb and shoulder surgery, hip fracture
Block failure, nerve injury, local anaesthetic toxicity, motor weakness and falls; interscalene block commonly causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy
Moderate to severe pain when oral analgesia is not possible
Patient controls timing, high satisfaction, flexible
Opioid effects (sedation, respiratory depression, nausea, pruritus), programming and device errors

blocks.title: Epidural haematoma and abscess
blocks.text: New or severe back pain, progressive leg numbness or weakness, or new bladder or bowel dysfunction in a patient with an epidural catheter (especially one receiving anticoagulants) must prompt immediate review, stopping the infusion and urgent MRI with neurosurgical referral. Outcome depends on decompression within hours. Timing of catheter insertion and removal relative to anticoagulant doses follows local protocol. Check against current BNF and local protocol.

items: Record observations, sensory level and motor block regularly (frequency per local protocol), and check pain scores at rest and on movement.
Inspect the insertion site and the catheter for leakage, migration or infection.
Look for unexpected high block (breathing difficulty, severe hypotension), signs of local anaesthetic toxicity (perioral tingling, tinnitus) and new back pain or neurological change.
Pay attention to pressure areas and safe mobilisation when motor block affects the legs.
Ensure the infusion bag and line are clearly labelled epidural, and use a dedicated pump and connectors that prevent intravenous connection.

blocks.markdown: **Patient-controlled analgesia (objective 2).** In PCA, the patient presses a button to deliver a small preset bolus of opioid (most commonly morphine intravenously) from a programmable pump, which gives immediate, individually titrated analgesia and a built-in safety mechanism: a sedated patient stops pressing the button. Safe use depends on correct programming, appropriate patient selection and education, a dedicated intravenous line with an anti-reflux valve, regular monitoring and an agreed rescue plan. Only the patient should press the button; PCA by proxy is unsafe.

rows: Small increments titrated to effect; teaching example 1 mg morphine
Continuous infusion in addition to demand doses
Usually avoided in opioid-naive adults because it removes the self-limiting safeguard
Maximum cumulative dose over a set time (for example 4 hours)
Initial dose given by clinician to establish analgesia
Titrated by clinician before PCA starts
blocks.caption: Typical PCA parameters (examples are illustrative; Check against current BNF and local protocol.)
Applies when no background infusion is programmed; a cumulative dose limit may lower the maximum further.

blocks.title: Maximum possible dose from a PCA setting
blocks.prompt: A PCA is programmed with morphine 1 mg bolus, 5 minute lockout, no background infusion and a 4-hour limit of 30 mg (teaching example). What is the theoretical maximum hourly and 4-hour dose?

steps.text: Maximum number of boluses per hour.

The 4-hour limit of 30 mg therefore becomes the effective ceiling and is a safety backstop. A patient who reaches it needs a clinician review and not a higher limit by default. Check against current BNF and local protocol.

blocks.answer: 12 mg per hour theoretical maximum; the 4-hour limit of 30 mg is the effective ceiling.

blocks.markdown: **Assessing pain and reassessing (objective 3).** Pain is subjective, so the patient's report is the gold standard. Common self-report tools are the numerical rating scale (0 to 10), the verbal rating scale (none, mild, moderate, severe) and the visual analogue scale; faces scales are used with young children; observational tools (for example the Abbey Pain Scale or PAINAD) are used with people unable to self-report, such as those with advanced dementia. Assess at rest and on movement or coughing, because functional pain decides whether physiotherapy and breathing exercises are possible. Treat and then reassess: record a score before, and again after the intervention at a time related to the drug's onset, then adjust. Look at sedation as well as pain, because a falling pain score with rising sedation is a warning. Distinguish a new, different or severe pain from the expected postoperative pain: it may signal a complication such as a compartment syndrome, bleeding or anastomotic leak and needs examination.

rows: Adults and older children able to self-report
Simple and widely used; conventional bands (mild, moderate, severe) vary between sources
Patients who prefer words to numbers
Based on behaviour such as facial expression and vocalisation

blocks.title: Interpreting PCA demand data and reassessing
blocks.prompt: A patient's PCA record shows 20 demands and 8 delivered boluses in the last hour, and a pain score of 6/10 on movement. What does this suggest and what should be done?

steps.text: Calculate the proportion of demands that delivered a bolus.
Interpret: many demands that fail because of the lockout suggest that analgesia is inadequate and that the patient is pressing repeatedly for relief.

Act: reassess pain at rest and movement and sedation, check the line and pump function, optimise non-opioid analgesia and regional options, and review the PCA settings with the pain team; do not simply remove the lockout.

blocks.answer: Only 40% of demands delivered: poor analgesia. Reassess, optimise multimodal analgesia and have the settings reviewed.

blocks.title: Pain on movement matters
blocks.text: A patient with a low resting pain score who cannot cough or mobilise has inadequate analgesia. Always ask about pain at rest and during activity.

points: Epidural analgesia and nerve blocks give targeted analgesia; complications include hypotension, motor block, nerve injury, toxicity and, rarely, epidural haematoma, which needs urgent MRI and decompression.
PCA delivers patient-triggered opioid boluses; the lockout interval, bolus size, dose limit and absence of a background infusion are safety features; only the patient presses the button.
Monitor pain scores, sedation, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, and verify settings against protocol.
Assess pain at rest and on movement with a suitable tool, reassess after every intervention, and investigate new or disproportionate pain.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has a thoracic epidural after a colectomy and receives prophylactic low molecular weight heparin. On day two she develops severe new back pain, increasing leg weakness and urinary retention. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Stop the epidural infusion and arrange urgent MRI and neurosurgical review
Reassure that this is normal motor block and observe overnight
Increase the infusion rate for better analgesia
Give a further dose of anticoagulant

questions.correctOptionText: Stop the epidural infusion and arrange urgent MRI and neurosurgical review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: suspected epidural haematoma or abscess is a surgical emergency.
distractorRationale.b: Motor block from the infusion should not increase with back pain and retention.
distractorRationale.c: Increasing the infusion would mask worsening cord compression.

questions.explanation: New back pain with progressive neurological deficit in a patient with an epidural, especially on anticoagulants, suggests spinal haematoma or abscess. Outcome depends on decompression within hours, so the infusion is stopped and imaging is arranged immediately.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has an ultrasound-guided interscalene block for shoulder surgery and becomes mildly breathless on the ward. Chest examination is otherwise normal. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Epidural haematoma
Total spinal anaesthesia
Ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy with hemidiaphragm paresis
Opioid overdose from the block

questions.correctOptionText: Ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy with hemidiaphragm paresis

distractorRationale.a: Epidural haematoma is unrelated to an interscalene block.
distractorRationale.b: Total spinal follows an intrathecal epidural dose, not a neck block.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: local anaesthetic spreads to the phrenic nerve in the neck, a common effect of interscalene block.
distractorRationale.d: The block does not contain opioid.

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve lies close to the brachial plexus at the interscalene level, so ipsilateral hemidiaphragm paresis is common. It is usually tolerated by healthy patients but may cause breathlessness, and the block is used cautiously in patients with limited respiratory reserve.

questions.stem: In a PCA pump, what is the purpose of the lockout interval?

options.text: It determines the opioid concentration
It sets a minimum time between boluses to limit the total dose delivered
It delivers a continuous background infusion
It allows the nurse to press the button on the patient's behalf

questions.correctOptionText: It sets a minimum time between boluses to limit the total dose delivered

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the lockout prevents repeated boluses in a short period.
distractorRationale.c: Background infusion is a separate setting and is usually avoided.
distractorRationale.d: Only the patient should press the button.

questions.explanation: The lockout is a safety feature limiting how fast a patient can self-administer opioid, giving time for each bolus to take effect before another is given. Together with a dose limit, it limits the maximum possible dose.

questions.stem: Why is a continuous background infusion generally avoided in opioid-naive adults on PCA?

options.text: It requires a larger syringe
It prevents the patient from pressing the button
It removes the self-limiting safeguard because the opioid continues to be delivered even if the patient becomes sedated
It makes the analgesia too weak

questions.correctOptionText: It removes the self-limiting safeguard because the opioid continues to be delivered even if the patient becomes sedated

distractorRationale.a: Syringe size is not the issue.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: the patient cannot reduce delivery by stopping pressing.
distractorRationale.d: Infusions would add analgesia rather than weaken it.

questions.explanation: The safety of PCA relies on a sedated patient ceasing to demand doses. A background infusion continues regardless of sedation and so increases the risk of accumulation and respiratory depression; local protocols define exceptions.

questions.stem: Which tool is most appropriate for assessing pain in a patient with advanced dementia who cannot give a numerical score?

options.text: Blood tests for pain markers
A visual analogue scale marked by the patient
An observational scale such as the Abbey Pain Scale or PAINAD
A numerical rating scale from 0 to 10

questions.correctOptionText: An observational scale such as the Abbey Pain Scale or PAINAD

distractorRationale.b: Requires understanding of the scale and self-report.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: observational tools assess behaviours such as facial expression and vocalisation.

questions.explanation: Patients unable to self-report still feel pain, so assessment uses observed behaviour and caregiver information. Treatment is then reassessed using the same tool.

questions.stem: A pain score taken at rest alone is sufficient to judge whether postoperative analgesia is adequate.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Pain on movement, deep breathing and coughing determines whether a patient can mobilise and clear secretions, and may be much higher than at rest. Both resting and dynamic scores are recorded, with reassessment after any intervention.

questions.stem: A PCA delivers morphine 1.5 mg per bolus with a 10 minute lockout and no background infusion. Calculate the maximum dose, in mg, that can be delivered in one hour (teaching example; check protocol).
questions.explanation: With a 10 minute lockout, up to 60 / 10 = 6 boluses can be delivered per hour. Each is 1.5 mg, so the maximum is 6 x 1.5 = 9 mg per hour, although a cumulative dose limit may reduce this.

questions.stem: In one hour a PCA records 24 patient demands, of which 9 delivered a bolus. Calculate the percentage of demands that delivered a bolus.
questions.explanation: The proportion is 9 / 24 = 0.375, or 37.5%. A low proportion with many demands suggests inadequate analgesia, so the patient should be reassessed rather than the lockout simply removed.

questions.stem: Discuss the complications of epidural analgesia and peripheral nerve blocks and the monitoring needed to detect them early.
markingGuide: Epidural: hypotension, motor block, urinary retention, pruritus or nausea with opioid, patchy or failed block
Dural puncture with headache, total spinal (high block, apnoea, hypotension)
Epidural haematoma or abscess: new back pain, leg weakness, bladder or bowel change; urgent MRI
Local anaesthetic toxicity: perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, arrhythmias
Peripheral blocks: block failure, nerve injury, falls from motor weakness, phrenic nerve palsy with interscalene block
Monitoring: regular observations, sensory and motor block, site inspection, pain scores, early review for new neurological change
questions.explanation: Most complications are detected by regular, structured observation and a low threshold for review. Haematoma and abscess are time-critical.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman rates pain 7/10 on movement and 3/10 at rest two hours after a knee replacement. Describe how you would assess, treat and reassess her pain.
markingGuide: Assess pain at rest and on movement with a numerical rating scale
Sedation score, observations, and look for complications or unusual pain
Treat with optimised multimodal analgesia (regular non-opioid analgesia, regional options) and opioid as needed per protocol
Reassess after the intervention at an appropriate interval and document
Escalate to the pain team if inadequate or if there are concerns
Check doses against BNF and local protocol
questions.explanation: Pain on movement determines function. Reassessment closes the loop and ensures that changes have worked and are safe.
